method_note: Combined run for prompts A1 (anatomy terms) and A2 (three temple types). Every quote was read this run through the archive.org search-inside API (fulltext/inside.php); fetched_url is that exact API URL, and the query term is in the q= parameter. The fetch tool was asked to relay the JSON 'text' strings character by character. Runs of spaces were collapsed to one space and IA_FTS_MATCH tags removed; OCR errors are kept (e.g. Bose 'masfaka' = mastaka, 'pisfa' = pista, 'bara'/'ham'/'barn' = bada, 'pirha'/'plrhds' = pidha, 'pafa' = pata, 'basanfa' = basanta, 'Kant' = Kani; Mitra 2003 'flatfish' = flattish, 'jagarnohana' = jagamohana; Mitra 1960 'khdkhard' = khakhara, 'pdbhdga' = pabhaga). 'scan leaf N' is the API page index, NOT the printed page. Kramrisch locators name the volume. BEHERA 2005 GLOSSARY CAVEAT: in its OCR the headwords and the definitions come back as separate hits on the same leaf, so pairing a definition with its headword is inferred from the alphabetical glossary layout (the headword was confirmed on the same leaf where noted). The fact-checker should open the PDF page to confirm those pairings. General definitions from research/ledgers/architecture.json (not yet fact-checked) were independently re-opened here; this ledger adds three sources that ledger lacked (Behera 2005 glossary and text, Debala Mitra's 1960 khakhara article, Kramrisch Vol. I on the rekha+pidha pair) and fills several of its gaps (pabhaga mouldings, khakhara name, bhumi, anuratha order). Site spellings are used in 'text'.

claims.text: Odisha's temples come in three main types: rekha, pidha and khakhara.

evidence.quote: The temples of Bhubaneswar, built over a span of more than five hundred years, can be resolved into three stylistic groups, viz., Rekha, Pidha and Khakhara orders.
The local Slipa Sastra texts mention three types of structures, rekha, pidha and khakara.
In Orissa, we find altogether four different types of temples, namely Rekha, Bhadra, KhakharS and Gouriya.

claims.conflicts: Bose 1932 counts FOUR types in Orissa, adding Gauriya, which he calls exotic (contents, scan leaf 14, q=Khakhara: 'Four different types— Rekha, Bhadra, KhakharS, Goufiya, the last an exotic'). Mitra (ASI) and Behera give three. The text says 'three main types', which fits all three sources.
claims.notes: Bose's name for the pidha type is 'Bhadra'. Mitra's sentence is about Bhubaneswar; Behera's is about the local silpa texts in general.

claims.text: These type names are old. Odisha's traditional building manuals, the silpa texts, already use them.

evidence.quote: In the construction of temples, Silpasastra texts are followed. The local Slipa Sastra texts mention three types of structures, rekha, pidha and khakara.
It may be useful to point out, at this stage, that in the silpasasfras, there are specifications of 55 Rekha, 6 Bhadra and 3 Khakhar3 temples.
In the canons of Orissan architecture it is known as the Pidha or Bhadra* type
In the Bhuvanapradipa,1 * an Orissan treatise on architecture, edited by N. K. Bose, the measurements and specifications of three different varieties of this kind of temples are given.

claims.conflicts: In the texts Bose edited, the pidha type is called 'Bhadra', not 'Pidha'. Mitra 1960 adds that the Bhuvanapradipa splits the khakhara into three varieties (Dravida, Badabhi, Kosoli).
claims.notes: Answers A2's question 'from the silpa texts, from Bose, or from modern scholars?': the names are in the silpa texts (per Bose, who edited them, and Behera). Scholarly, not established, because the manuscripts themselves were not opened (Silpa Prakasa is catalogue-only).

claims.text: A rekha deula has a tall, curved tower. The tower rises almost straight at first, then curves inward more and more near the top.

evidence.quote: rekha deul order of temple characterised by a curvilinear tower which presents the appearance of a continuous line
The gandi of the Rekha rises straight up to a short height and then begins to curve inwards at an increasing rate.

evidence.locator: scan leaf 171, glossary (printed page unverified; headword pairing inferred, see method_note)
evidence.quote: order of temple characterized by a curvilinear tower; this type of structure is usually limited to the main temple.

claims.notes: Bose (same leaf) adds that the cross-section of the tower is square at every height and compares the outline to 'a tall bamboo -post which has been slightly bent towards the top by a rope'. Mitra spells 'rekha deul'.

claims.text: The rekha form is usually used for the main shrine, the sanctuary.

evidence.locator: scan leaf 171, glossary (printed page unverified; headword pairing inferred, see method_note)
evidence.quote: order of temple characterized by a curvilinear tower; this type of structure is usually limited to the main temple.
The main temple or the Vimana (also called deula) is of the rekha order and has a curvilinear superstructure.

evidence.locator: Vol. I, scan leaf 227 (printed page unverified)
evidence.quote: The closed volume of an Orissan temple consists of the Prasada and its Man^apa; the former is the Rekha or Bara Deul and the latter is the Pirha Deul; its superstructure is pyramidal
The sanctuary proper is a rekha deul or bada deul but is no longer extant.

claims.notes: Mitra's sentence is about Konark only; Behera and Kramrisch state the general pattern. No ASI source states the general rule, so scholarly. Kramrisch OCR 'Man^apa' = Mandapa, 'Pirha' = pidha.

claims.text: A pidha deula has a roof like a stepped pyramid. It is built from flat layers, called pidhas, that get smaller as they rise.

evidence.quote: pidha deul temple of which the pyramidal roof is made of pidhas
In Bhadra temples, the gandi is composed of a number of plrhds or horizontal platforms, piled up in the form of a pyramid.
The pidhas diminish in size as they rise and generally the uppermost pidha is half the size of the lowest one.

claims.notes: Bose calls this type 'Bhadra'; OCR 'plrhds' = pirhas (pidhas).

claims.text: The pidha form is mostly used for a temple's halls: the jagamohana, the dance hall and the hall of offerings.

evidence.quote: this form of structure is usually limited to the jagamohana, bhoga-mandapa and nata-mandapa in Orissa
The frontal porch or the jagamohana (also called mukhamandapa, mukhasala, bhadradeula, etc) meant for sheltering the devotees, is a pidha deula, possessing a pyramidal superstructure.
it is known as the Pidha or Bhadra* type which is first found as the porch of the main iikkara or rekha temples and then as an independent unit

claims.notes: Panigrahi OCR 'iikkara' = sikhara. Behera (scan leaf 106, q=pidha) adds that Konark's eastern gateway 'was apparently a pidha temple', so gateways could also take this form; not put in text.

claims.text: The pidha hall came a little later. In the earliest temples, the hall in front had a flatter roof, not a stepped pyramid.

evidence.quote: In the earlier phase of the style there was no pidha deula and the jagamohana was distinguished by a flat roof, but in course of time, this was changed into a pyramidal one.
resembles a type of temple which was definitely of late origin at Bhubaneswar and appears for the first time, as the porch of the Mukte^vara much later in date than the ParaSuramesvara.
Its jagamohana has become a pidha deula with pidhas arranged in a continous succession and crowned by a kalasa.

claims.conflicts: Behera says the early hall had 'a flat roof'; Panigrahi calls the early porch 'a low mandapa' (OCR 'tnattdapa'). The Parasuramesvara ledger (parasuramesvara-2) has other descriptions of that hall's roof (two-stage sloping / double roof) — hence 'flatter' in the text, not 'flat'.
claims.notes: Behera leaf 59's sentence is about the Mukteshvara. No date is put in the text.

claims.text: A pidha hall is also called a bhadra deula or a mukhasala (front hall).

evidence.quote: The Bhadra is also called the MukhasSilS (lit. the building which is placed to wards the face or front of the Rekha), or Pijrha temple on account of its gandi being composed of pirhas.
bhadra deul auspicious temple; it refers to the porch in front of a sanctuary

evidence.locator: scan leaf 170, glossary (printed page unverified; headword not shown in the hit)
evidence.quote: 'front hall; pidha temple infront of the sanctuary; also known as jagamohana.

claims.notes: Behera leaf 50 also lists 'mukhamandapa, mukhasala, bhadradeula' as names of the jagamohana (quote in anat-006). Mitra glosses bhadra as 'auspicious'.

claims.text: A khakhara deula has an oblong (rectangular) plan. Its roof is long and rounded on top, like half a barrel lying on its side.

evidence.quote: (1) the ground-plan of the Rekha and Bhadra is square, while
(2) that of the Khskhar9 is rectangular.
The khakhra temple, used for Devi worship, is characterized by oblong bada and semi- cylindrical roof.
The form of the roof of the khdkhard temples is a modified survival of the primitive halls with a semi-cylindrical roof
representations of shrines with wagon- vaulted roofs ( khakhara - mundis) in close succession.

claims.notes: Bose's two OCR hits are parts of one sentence on leaf 100. Bose leaf 108 (q=rectangular) adds 'The cross-section all through is however rectangular.' Mitra 1960 (leaf 22) also calls the Vaital's top 'the clear-cut shape of a semi-cylinder'.

claims.text: Scholars think this roof copies very old halls whose rounded roofs were made of timber or bent bamboo.

evidence.quote: a modified survival of the primitive halls with a semi-cylindrical roof resting on a framework of timber6 * or bent split bamboos (in the case of a thatched roof)
Thus, this member resembles very closely the lower portion of the roof of the traditional chaitya-hall

claims.conflicts: Percy Brown and Panigrahi also derive the Vaital Deul's roof from the Buddhist chaitya-hall (architecture.json arch-019; not re-opened in this run). Panigrahi also reports M.M. Ganguly's view that it comes from the rathas of Mahabalipuram (arch-019 conflicts). Mitra 1960 (leaf 10) says there is 'no basis to think that the khakhara temples of Bhubaneswar are South Indian in inspiration'.
claims.notes: An interpretation, attributed to scholars. '6 *' is a footnote marker in the OCR.

claims.text: The name khakhara comes from a long gourd called kakharu in Odia. The temple's roof looks a little like it.

evidence.quote: The name khdkhara, given by the Orissan Gilpin to this type, is due to the faint resemblance of the barrel-vaulted elongated roof of its temples with a variety of pumpkin-gourd, called kakhdru in Oriya.

claims.conflicts: The research report calls the kakharu a 'pumpkin'; Mitra says 'a variety of pumpkin-gourd'. The text says 'gourd'.
claims.notes: Single source, so scholarly. OCR 'Gilpin' = silpin (craftsman). Mitra (same passage) adds the variety is called vaita-kakharu ('boat-shaped'), and that 'vaitala' is 'no doubt at the root of the nomenclature of the Vait&l Deul' — a possible fun fact for the Vaital Deul, not claimed here. The architecture.json ledger listed this name origin as not found; this fills it.

claims.text: Scholars link khakhara temples with the worship of goddesses (Shakti). But goddesses are also found in temples of other types.

evidence.quote: The available evidence thus indicates that temples of this Order in Orissa belonged to the Sakta cult,6 * though the converse is not true, for Sakti is also seen en¬ shrined in temples of other Orders
The khakhra temple, used for Devi worship, is characterized by oblong bada and semi- cylindrical roof.

claims.conflicts: Mitra 1960: all khakhara temples she knew were Sakta, but goddesses also sit in rekha temples (Mohini, Chitrakarini). Behera 2005: 'used for Devi worship'. Percy Brown 1959 calls the Vaital Deul 'a Siva temple of the Orissan group' (Brown, scan leaf 240, q=deul; the relayed string may be normalised, so it is kept here rather than as evidence; architecture.json arch-017 has the same quote). Research report says 'reserved mainly for Shakta/goddess temples'.
claims.notes: Tier uncertain because Brown disagrees for the type-site. Mitra's own wording ('the available evidence thus indicates') is cautious. Respectful framing: the text says 'scholars link', not 'khakhara temples are for goddesses'.

claims.text: Two well-known khakhara temples are the Vaital Deul and the small Gauri temple, both in Bhubaneswar.

evidence.quote: The gandi of the KhakharS is composed either like that of a Rekha as in the Vaital temple in Bhubaneswar or like that of a Bhadra, with certain minor differences, as in the temple of Gauri in the same village.
The small Gauri temple is of the Khakhara type which is akin to the Vaitil temple in its architecture, and thus represents a different architectural conception.
Class I is well represented by the Vaital Deul (Pl. VI A) of Bhubaneswar.

claims.notes: Mitra 1960 describes further khakhara temples, including the Varahi temple at Chaurasi (leaf 11, q=Sakta: 'The neglected temple ... of Chaurasi, called the Vfir&hl'), but that sentence does not itself say 'khakhara' (it is inside her article on khakhara temples), so Varahi is kept out of the text. No dates are claimed here (Vaital dates differ by source; see architecture.json arch-018).

claims.text: Full khakhara temples are rare. But small carved models of them, called khakhara-mundis, decorate the walls of many other temples.

evidence.quote: Though the khakhara-mundi (Pis. XII B and C and XIII) is a very common decorative motif on Orissan temples of both the Rekha and Pitfd Orders, khdkhara temples are rather rare1 in Orissa.
khakhara-mundi miniature representation of a khakhara temple as an ornamental motif
When a niche is surmounted by pidha type of temples, it is called pidha-mundi; when it is provided with a crowning structure of khakhara type, it is called khakhara-mundi.

claims.notes: Bose 1932 counts six khakhara examples in Bhubaneswar (architecture.json arch-015; not re-opened here). Pidha-mundi (Mitra leaf 101: 'pidha-mundi miniature representation of a pidha temple as an ornamental motif') could be a sibling glossary entry.

claims.text: A typical Odisha temple joins two types. A rekha tower rises over the shrine, and a pidha hall stands in front of it.

evidence.quote: A rekha deul is characterised by a curvilinear tower, while the front porch called jagarnohana or bhadra deul, where the devotees assemble, is a pidha deul,

In front of the deul is a square building or assembly hall corresponding to the mandapa in other parts, but here known as the jagamohan. These two edifices combined constitute the essentials of the Orissan temple type.
In the Orissan style of temple architecture, however, the two together make the temple a complete whole. The two structures are linked internally.

evidence.locator: Vol. I, scan leaf 227 (printed page unverified)
evidence.quote: The closed volume of an Orissan temple consists of the Prasada and its Man^apa; the former is the Rekha or Bara Deul and the latter is the Pirha Deul

claims.notes: Mitra's sentence is about Konark; Brown, Behera and Kramrisch state it generally. Behera (same leaf) contrasts 'the vertical ascent of the curvilinear tower' with 'the horizontal emphasis of the jagamohana' — usable for a kid-friendly 'tall vs wide' line.

claims.text: Deula is the local word for a temple. Used alone, it often means just the main shrine with its tower.

evidence.quote: deul general name for a temple as a whole; when used singly, it refers to the sanctuary as distinguished from the porch or festive hall
The generic name for a temple is deal, but as the building in the first instance consisted very often of a sanctuary only, the same word was employed for this tower- like structure also.
Dewlf deal, in Bengal and Orissa generic name for a temple as a whole, but it is also used to signify the sanctuary only, such as the cella and its tower, the vimana.

claims.notes: Spellings: deul (Mitra, Brown; OCR 'deal'), deula (Behera), Deul (Kramrisch). Brown's glossary also gives 'Dewl'.

claims.text: The main shrine is also called the bada deula, which means 'big temple'.

evidence.quote: bada deul literally big temple, meaning the sanctuary
Externally the jagamohana is subordinate to the main temple (bada deula) in height.

evidence.locator: Vol. I, scan leaf 227 (printed page unverified)
evidence.quote: the former is the Rekha or Bara Deul and the latter is the Pirha Deul

claims.notes: IMPORTANT for the builder: 'bada' in 'bada deula' (big) is a different word from 'bada' (wall, anat-026) in roman spelling. Kramrisch writes 'Bara Deul'; Bose writes the wall as 'bara'. The glossary should explain both to avoid confusion.

claims.text: The main shrine with its tower is also called the vimana.

evidence.quote: The main temple or the Vimana (also called deula) is of the rekha order and has a curvilinear superstructure.
it is also used to signify the sanctuary only, such as the cella and its tower, the vimana.

claims.notes: No ASI source defines 'vimana' in the passages read, so scholarly. Brown (scan leaf 214) says the Deul corresponds 'to the Vimana in other parts' (architecture.json arch-032; that exact phrase was not re-relayed this run).

claims.text: The jagamohana is the hall in front of the main shrine, where worshippers gather. It usually has a pidha (stepped) roof.

evidence.quote: jagamohana hall in front of a sanctuary, usually in a pidha temple.
Jagamohan—That which pleases the whole world ; that which is most pleasing ; name of structure in front of Rekha* usually a Bhadra.
the front porch called jagarnohana or bhadra deul, where the devotees assemble, is a pidha deul,
The frontal porch or the jagamohana (also called mukhamandapa, mukhasala, bhadradeula, etc) meant for sheltering the devotees, is a pidha deula, possessing a pyramidal superstructure.

claims.notes: Group: structure. Early jagamohanas were not pidha (anat-007), hence 'usually'. Mitra leaf 92 calls it 'the hall of congregation'.

claims.text: The word jagamohana is explained as 'that which pleases the whole world'.

evidence.quote: Jagamohan—That which pleases the whole world ; that which is most pleasing ;

claims.notes: Single source (Bose's glossary), so scholarly.

claims.text: The natamandira is the dance hall. In large temples it stands in front of the jagamohana.

evidence.quote: The two buildings usually supplemented were first the Nat~Mandir or Dancing Hall, and secondly in front of this the Bhog Mamlir or Hall of Offerings.
nata mandapa or the dancing hall;

evidence.locator: scan leaf 170, glossary (printed page unverified; headword 'Nata-mandira' confirmed on the same leaf via q=mandira)
evidence.quote: dancing hall of a temple.

claims.conflicts: Names differ: natamandira / Nata-mandira (Behera), nata-mandapa (Mitra), Nat Mandir (Brown). Mitra's glossary glosses nata-mandapa as 'festive hall' (scan leaf 101, q=mandapa: 'nata-mandapa festive hall'), while her Lingaraja text and Brown and Behera say 'dancing hall'.
claims.notes: Brown (same leaf) says these halls were added 'to the front of the assembly hall' as ritual developed. Group: structure.

claims.text: The bhogamandapa is the hall of offering. It usually stands in front of the dance hall.

evidence.quote: bhoga-mandapa hall of offering

evidence.locator: scan leaf 167, glossary (printed page unverified; headword 'Bhoga-mandapa' confirmed on the same leaf via q=bhoga)
evidence.quote: 'hall of offering'; the refectory hall of a temple; the structure is usually found in front of the nata mandira.
Bhoga-mandapa, the refectory hall of a temple (Orissa).

claims.conflicts: At Konark the naming of the detached hall in front differs: Mitra (scan leaf 70, q=mandapa) says it 'is generally believed to be a nata-mandapa (festive hall)', but elsewhere calls a pillared hall there 'the bhoga-mandapa' (scan leaf 29, q=bada). This affects Konark labels, not the general definition.
claims.notes: 'Refectory' (Brown, Behera) means a dining hall; the text keeps to 'hall of offering'. Group: structure.

claims.field: elements (structure order); academy (how a complex is laid out)
claims.text: In the largest temples, four buildings stand in one straight line: deula, jagamohana, natamandira and bhogamandapa. The two front halls were often added later.

evidence.quote: The Lingaraja consists of the customary four structures - the deul called the Sri Mandir; jagamohana or the hall of congregation; nata mandapa or the dancing hall; and bhoga-mandapa or the hall of offerings.
All these buildings are disposed on the same axis but do not necessarily belong to the same period.
it consists of four edifices in one alignment - the rekha deul , jagamohana and the later additions of the nata and bhoga- mandapas.
other buildings were found necessary, and were added to the front of the assembly hall, thus presenting in the larger examples a series of structures all in one axial alignment.

claims.notes: Mitra leaf 92 is Lingaraja, leaf 86 Jagannatha (Puri); Brown leaf 212 is general. Behera (scan leaf 59, q=pidha) also says Lingaraja has 'deula, jagamohana, natamandira and bhogamandapa in one axial alignment'. Mitra calls the four 'customary'.

claims.text: From bottom to top, a temple has four parts: the pista (platform), bada (wall), gandi (tower or roof) and mastaka (crown).

evidence.quote: The body of all these temples can be divided along the vertical axis into four principal parts namely, the pisfa or the pedestal, the bara or the wall, the gandi or the body and the masfaka or the crown.
Both the sanctuary and the porch are divided into four broad parts along the vertical plane. These are the pishta or platform, the bada or vertical wall, the gandi or the curvilinear tower
Both structures can be divided into four parts along the vertical plane. The four divisions are pitha, bada, gandi and shira or mastaka.

claims.conflicts: Mitra 1960 (scan leaf 22, q=semi-cylindrical) speaks of 'the three well-known divisions of the Orissan rekha and pidd deals—bada, gandi and nuistaka', leaving out the platform. Percy Brown 1959 (scan leaf 212, q=generic) uses different names for the tower parts: 'the tall middle portion or chhapra, the flat fluted disc at the summit known as the artda, and its finial or kalasa'.
claims.notes: Mitra's sentence continues on leaf 26: 'roof in the case of a pidha deul and the mast aka which is the head or crowning elements.' Spellings of the platform: pista (Bose, Brown), pishta (Mitra), pitha (Behera).

claims.text: The pista is the platform or base that a temple stands on. Not every temple has one.

evidence.quote: pishta platform
Pisfa^ Pifha, Prisfha — Pedestal (examples, Padma, Singha, Bhadra, Bedi, Suthira, Khura, Kumbha, Parijangha, Kurma).
Standing on a basement or a plinth (pista), these halls were invariably of one story only
It has no platform and is tri-ratha in plan.

claims.notes: Mitra leaf 88 is about the Parasuramesvara (so 'not every temple has one'). Behera's glossary (scan leaf 171, q=platform) has 'pedestal; stylobate; platform', presumably under 'Pitha' (pairing inferred). Bose lists nine named kinds of pista from the silpa texts (leaf 118). Group: vertical-division.

claims.text: The bada is the upright wall of the temple. It stands between the platform and the tower or roof.

evidence.quote: bada enclosure; wall; vertical portion of a temple above pishta and below spire or roof
Wall ; portion between pis(a and gan^i of a temple.

evidence.locator: scan leaf 166, glossary (printed page unverified; headword pairing inferred)
evidence.quote: 'wall', vertical part of a temple between pitha and gandi.

claims.notes: Bose spells 'bara' (his glossary hit shows only the definition). Do not confuse with 'bada deula' (big temple), anat-017. Group: vertical-division.

claims.text: The gandi is the main body of the tower or roof, above the wall. The word means 'trunk', as in the trunk of a body.

evidence.quote: gandi literally trunk; curvilinear spire or pyramidal roof above bada and below the mastaka of a temple
The gandi (lit. the trunk of the body) or the curvilinear tower is composed of different elements along the various pagas.

evidence.locator: scan leaf 168, glossary (printed page unverified; headword 'Gandi' confirmed on the same leaf via q=gandi)
evidence.quote: trunk, curvilinear spire or pyramidal roof between the bada and mastaka of a temple.

claims.conflicts: Percy Brown 1959 calls the tall middle portion of the tower the 'chhapra' (scan leaf 212, q=generic), not gandi.
claims.notes: Bose glossary (leaf 287, q=Trunk) also defines where the gandi ends in each type: 'in Rekha, portion between bara and bisama ; in Bhadra, between bara and behi'. Group: vertical-division.

claims.text: The mastaka is the crown: the stack of round parts on top of the tower. The word means 'head'.

evidence.quote: mastaka head; crowning elements above the gandi of a temple

evidence.locator: scan leaf 170, glossary (printed page unverified; headword 'Mastaka' appears on the same leaf via q=mandira)
evidence.quote: 'head'; crowning elements above the gandi of a temple
The masfaka of the Rekha starts from above the gandi. It is composed of several elements, which are all circular in cross-section.

claims.conflicts: Bose says 'mastaka' is not a traditional silpa term but one coined for convenience: 'The masfaka (a name which has been coined for the sake of convenience)' (scan leaf 134, q=coined) and glossary 'Masfaka — Name coined to denote portion of a temple above gan4i and below kalasa,' (scan leaf 289, q=coined). Mitra and Behera treat it as the standard term meaning 'head'. Behera also gives 'shira' as an alternative (anat-024).
claims.notes: The conflict is about the word's origin, not the part; the fact-checker may lower to scholarly or add 'a name scholars use'. Mitra leaf 26: 'While the mastaka is circular in cross-section, the bada and gandi are square internally in horizontal sections.' Group: vertical-division.

claims.field: glossary (body names); academy.why_questions (body names) — supporting only
claims.text: Many part names come from the human body, such as foot, shin, trunk, throat and head. Scholars say the temple was pictured as a body.

evidence.quote: It is clear from a study of the above terms that the Rekha temple has been likened to the human body.
The naming of these elements after human limbs ( mastaka , for instance, is head) suggests that temples were likened to the human body.
Therefore the different parts of the temple are named after limbs of the body.

claims.conflicts: Body-word translations differ for jangha (anat-036).
claims.notes: Interpretation, so scholarly. Behera (same leaf) goes further: 'The Orissan craftsmen considered the temple as the body of the Cosmic Being.' That belongs to the why-this-shape topic and must stay attributed (Behera; cf. Kramrisch's Purusha, architecture.json arch-026). Bose (leaf 134) links the body idea to a craftsmen's male/female saying; left out here (not needed, and must be handled neutrally if used).

claims.text: The pabhaga is the 'foot' of the wall. It is a band of three to five stone mouldings at the bottom of the wall.

evidence.quote: Division corresponding to the foot ; set of three, four or five mouldings at the base of a temple (above pis(a or pedestal).

evidence.locator: scan leaf 170, glossary (printed page unverified; headword pairing inferred)
evidence.quote: 'foot part'; division of the wall corresponding to the foot of the bada; a set of mouldings forming the lowest part of the bada of a temple.
the bada of this temple has five divisions - the lowest being the pabhaga,

claims.notes: Bose's glossary hit shows the definition without its headword; Bose leaf 133 names it: 'the pabhaga or the division corresponding to the foot (i. e. the base)'. Overlap: parasuramesvara-2 claim 008 cites the same Bose leaf 290 for this temple. Parent: bada. Group: bada-part.

claims.text: In fully developed temples, the foot of the wall has five mouldings, named khura, kumbha, pata, kani and basanta. Early temples may have fewer.

evidence.quote: The ratio of the different mouldings of the pabha^ja, viz. the kbura, kumhfia, pafa, kani and basanfa will be according to one of the following tables
The pdbhdga consists, as in the fully developed Orissan temples, of the khurd, kumbha, pafd, kani and pafa- like basmnta, the first, third and fifth of them carved.
As usual in Orissan temples, pabhaga consists of five mouldings,
the bada, like that of the early group of Bhubaneswar, has three parts—pabhdga of four mouldings, jangha and varanda

claims.conflicts: Names of the second moulding vary. Bose's translation of a silpa text (scan leaf 264, q=mouldings) lists 'the khura, including tnachuH ... the kalasa ... the pafa ... the kani ... the basanfa' — kalasa in place of kumbha; Bose's glossary (leaf 288, q=water-pot) says kalasa can '(rarely)' mean 'the moulding known as kumbha'. The details page (fetched) shows title 'JOURNAL OF THE ASIATIC SOCIETY VOL. 2, NO. 1-4', date 1960, publisher 'ASIATIC SOCIETY, CALCUTTA', creator 'N.A'. The article title appears at scan leaf 9 ('FOUR LITTLE-KNOWN KHAKHARA TEMPLES OF ORISSA') with 'By Debala Mitra' (leaf 9) and 'By Mrs. Deb ala Mitra' in the contents (leaf 7). The journal SERIES (e.g. Fourth Series) and the printed page range were NOT confirmed; a search for 'Fourth Series' returned no hit. The article refers to its own 'p. 2' for the Bhuvanapradipa passage that sits on scan leaf 10, suggesting the article starts at printed p. 1, but that is an inference. Leaves 52-60 duplicate leaves 22-30 in the scan. HUMAN APPROVAL NEEDED: new source; also decide whether the Journal of the Asiatic Society counts as a peer-reviewed journal for this site.
